en: The title card reads *Ācaryakriyāsamuccaya* (sic!). There are six paper leaves, but only two belong to the *Ācaryakriyāsamuccaya*. The remainder is from a work by Divākarendra (also known as Divākaracandra) titled *Daśākuśalakarmaphalaniścaya*, consisting of eleven chapters. An exact copy of the missing first folio can be found separately in Cambridge (Add. 1598 and Add. [1599]).

For an edition of the first [text], see Ratna Handurukande, “Daśākuśalakarmaphala,” in: *Kalyāṇī*, Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of Kelaniya, Vols. V and VI, pp. 43–48, 1986–1987. RH did not have access to the latter; in fact, Add. 1585 (now available in color) is the missing first folio of the NAK manuscript.
This is numbered 13v (our text begins here, indicating that it was in a composite manuscript together with the *Sumāgadhāvadāna*); the NAK manuscript continues up to folio 17.
Handurukande’s edition reads as follows:
*namo buddhāya*.

Having bowed to the Jina— the Lord of the World who has conquered all faults, who is rich in compassion, and who proclaims the efficacy of karma— I shall explain the fruit born of the ten unwholesome actions.
In the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna*, the Blessed One himself declared that the ten unwholesome paths of action are the causes for rebirth in the miserable states. (2)
Action of the body is threefold, that of speech is fourfold, and that of the mind is of three kinds; these are the ten paths of action. (3)
Taking life, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct—these three types of action constitute the bodily [karma] of humans when they possess five factors. (4)
False speech, slander, harsh words, and frivolous chatter—
this fourfold action is known by the wise as verbal karma. (5)
Covetousness, hatred toward sentient beings, and wrong view—these three constitute all mental action; they should be avoided by those who seek what is wholesome. (6)
Whatever action—whether good or bad—has been performed by body, speech, or mind, one reaps its fruit oneself; the world is not governed by a Lord.
The wise say that the fruit produced by karma is not created by Īśvara or other such [causes].
That [fruit] should be understood by the discerning precisely in the sequence that is about to be explained. (8)
O birds, as embodied beings are being burned by fire in hell,
those who move amidst the flames pierce their skull-bowls and drink their blood. (9)
Those birds with sharp beaks that move within the skull-bowl— having pierced the head and then the brain, they drink it as if it were molten fire. 10.
Having torn open their own tongues, those birds, who feed on the flesh of tongues and resemble Rākṣasas,
devour them repeatedly from all sides. || 11 ||
And even after eating, that tongue becomes joined with the wind;
it is soft, dry, broad-tipped, and as delicate as a lotus petal.
Soft and subtle,
they fall upon those of unsubdued mind, known by the name "tooth-extractor," [and] those named after food.
Having violently torn out the teeth, they devour the flesh located therein.
Having scratched his throat with their claws,
the birds, who pull at the vessels of the neck, joyfully tore out the windpipe and began devouring it.
First, having torn open the belly, the birds that dwell in the *kloman* tear it apart with their beaks and,
having carved out the tender *kloman*, they devour the nearby heart-flesh.
Birds with gaping mouths and harsh beaks, nameless and devoid of strength, strike the stomach and devour it.
There are powerful birds called Plīhasaṃkartakas who, having exposed the spleen, always consume it from the sky. || 17 ||
And those birds, swift as the wind, that feed upon the entrails—
scattering them and tearing out the intestines without remainder— they enjoy them while soaring through the sky. (18)
Known as the "Backbone-Dwellers," they are endowed with piercing cries and great strength;
crushing with their beaks, they peck at the spinal columns of embodied beings. (19)
The birds known as *marmāvaghaṭṭakas* devour the flesh, just like ordinary birds; having pierced the vital organs, these terrifying creatures feast upon the marrow.
Even the swift steeds, though afflicted by thirst, drink from the mouth of a needle's eye.
[14v] ...steadfastly from passion for the bodies that are the maws of hell. And there are fierce creatures that move within the cavities of the bones, bringing an end to the world.

Together they constantly consume the exceedingly intense and delicious essence of the Kaikeyas. Afflicted by hunger, these skin-eaters strip away all their hides with sharp pincers of their beaks and devour them piece by piece.
Those known as meat-eaters are *yātudhānas* who lie in wait;
intoxicated by their own lust, they tear away the succulent flesh and devour it.
With their beaks, they crush the tips of branches and the hands and feet into fragments.

The birds known as *nakhanikṛntakas* clip off all their nails. [1.25] Those called *medodas*, the deluded, talkative, sky-dwellers, having abandoned the flesh, eat the fat together with their siblings. [1.26]
Those servants of Kṛtānta known as "Sinew-Extractors" seize the mass of sinews with pincers and are dragged away by those winged creatures.
Those known as "Hair-Balls," possessing beaks a yojana long—
They uproot the wicked ones while shedding blood, along with their prey.
Likewise, for three thousand yojanas down in the Avīci hell,
they are devoured by great birds known as the Mahābhairava yakṣas and by other birds.
Even if living beings have been devoured for thousands of millions of years,
those of sinful nature are born again and again through their defiled karma. If, by some chance, one who possesses an unwholesome mind should be released from that state, [he would still fall back].
Surrounded by nets of suffering, seeking protection from another source—
[1.31] Enveloped by eleven blazing masses of fire, bound by the noose of karma, he runs through the wilderness. [1.32]
There, that great sinner is tormented by powerful adversaries who wield various weapons and cry out, "O protector!
As he flees from there, he falls into a narrow chasm.
At the very moment it falls into that [womb], its sequence becomes liquefied.
Having developed feet, it again undergoes contact with the mother;
overwhelmed by sensation, it once more becomes of such a state. [1.34–1.35]
Then, rising up again by the power of former karma as he proceeds from there,
a terrifying and bottomless great abyss appears before him.
Lacking all strength, he falls into it, which is filled with many weapons.
At the end of thousands of millions of years, he is tossed up by the wind,
his limbs smeared with flowing blood and his face distorted by agony.
Standing on the bank, crying out with indistinct words, he suddenly faints.
Then, through contact with the wind, that denizen of hell regains consciousness.
Terrified by fear, the hell-being is devoured by vultures, herons, crows, and ravens. [1.39]
Having somehow escaped from there, he wanders through the place called the Cakrāṅkavivara and,
being helpless, enters the most dreadful *bhramaccakra* (whirling wheel). There,
the sharp and vast [blades] with adamantine hubs blaze intensely.
As he stands there, wheels fall upon the head of that evil-minded one. With his limbs shattered, he proceeds along a narrow path;
unable to withstand the assault, he climbs the mountain.
Having reached the mountain named Mārkoṭaka,
he is devoured for a long time by many creatures called mārkoṭakas who are exceedingly voracious.
Furthermore, by the power of karma, his flesh grows back soft once again.
In that very same way, it is devoured again, and it manifests once more.
As it has been stated in due order, the perpetrator of the taking of life experiences the terrible fruit born of karma for many tens of millions of eons. [1.44–1.45]
Realizing that the fruit of taking life is terrible, a wise person of good intellect should always abandon the harming of living beings.
The intellect should be applied for the benefit of all sentient beings toward enlightenment, since that is the root of all that is auspicious; such is this [teaching]. [1.46] (Vasantatilakā)
Thus ends the first chapter, the exposition on the fruit of taking life, in the *Daśākuśalakarmaphalaniścaya* (The Determination of the Fruits of the Ten Unwholesome Actions). || o ||
It is like a city of the Gandharvas, a mirage, or water in the moon; it consists of various kinds of gold and silver of many distinct qualities.
That person who performs unwholesome deeds beholds wealth consisting of gems, garments, ornaments, coral, and pearls, as well as water and the moon. [2.1]
With his mental faculties deluded by his own past karma, he thinks, "All this wealth is mine."
Having observed this, the hunter proceeds,
indeed leaping over the pit of fire dense with flickering sparks.
There, his mass of hair is pulled out and he is bound with firm nooses by those known as the servants of Yama, produced by his own karma.
With a piteous cry and his slender body trembling,
he is cast into a place of blazing weapons;
having struck him down with violence, he is burned once again.

This thief of another's property has his noble body torn apart by Deaths with the blades of sharpened swords, and his limbs are sawn asunder with keen saws until his body is reduced to mere bones. [2.4]
Furthermore, through the process of breathing and by the force of its own karma, soft and flaccid flesh is produced once again.
For such a person as this, craving increases even further toward material wealth; he remains exactly the same as before.
Distressed by the fruit of taking what is not given because of his lack of faith, [he continues in that state].
A wise person should abandon the wealth of others;
moreover, they should especially cultivate a mind devoted to giving.
For through giving, people everywhere shall be happy. [2.6]
This is the "Indravajrā" [verse] concerning the exposition of the fruit of taking what is not given, from the *Daśākuśalakarmaphalaniścaya*.
The Second Chapter. || 0 ||
One whose inner self has strayed through blameworthy desires, accompanied by suffering, destined for an evil rebirth, and deluded— (cf. 2.1060–1069)
Beholding a delightful region adorned with various trees, the lover approaches it. [3.1] (Upajāti)
Resembling a dream or a magical illusion, she was joyful, endowed with youth, beautiful, and possessed of excellent limbs.
There he beholds her, agitated by passion, displaying gestures and movements produced by her karma;
having seen her again, his passion aroused, he runs toward her.
Having plunged into that blazing pit of glowing coals,
his consciousness was utterly destroyed by his own evil deeds.
Having reached her, she reveals her true nature:
having arrived, she— her body made of iron, with blazing and fierce fangs— embraces him tightly.
Becoming exceedingly terrifying with blazing, fierce fangs and letting out a loud, mocking laugh, she begins to devour him as he greedily bites his lip. [3.4]
Having reduced him to mere bones, she abandons him;
yet upon being abandoned, his flesh grows back,
and thus his passion increases all the more.
She too eats the flesh that has grown there again. For such a person as this, a thousand eons pass by before the destruction of their evil is reached.
Furthermore, who would eat one whose passion has increased,
and who would tear him to pieces with teeth and claws? The Buddhas proclaim that this is the root of ruin.
A woman in the three worlds possesses amorous gestures; therefore, she should be avoided with great effort, for a beautiful woman is as crooked as a female serpent when indulged in pleasure. [3.7]
O grateful ones, quickly abandon the improper pursuit of sensual desires;
practice celibacy, the source of all happiness.
The discerning person dwells in the sublime celestial palaces of the Brahma-world.
Having experienced the bliss of tranquility and having thereby abandoned the afflictions. [3.8]
Thus ends the third chapter, the exposition on sexual misconduct, in the Determination of the Fruits of the Ten Unwholesome Actions. ||o||
By the power of karma, having found a person who spoke falsehoods in hell, [he is seized] by the messengers of Yama.
Having gaped its mouth wide open,
its tongue is forcibly pulled out;
and that [tongue] is [subjected to this] by the power of its own karma.
It is five hundred yojanas in extent;
having been seized, it is placed by them upon the heated ground of iron. [4.2]
There, born of unwholesome karma, are terrifying and powerful bulls;
their horns are sharp and exceedingly blazing.
And a thousand ploughs prevail there,
driven by bulls.
The messengers of Yama carry him on their thousand heads,
and that evil-souled one cries out most bitterly, overwhelmed by intense agony.
There flows a river carrying forth a continuous stream of pus, blood,
and worms.
Foul-smelling, putrid, and dangerous,
with great force, it remains for a thousand eons;
then, somehow, within the cavity of the mouth—
A soft, red tongue enters his mouth;
having risen, it then follows him wherever he goes—therein lies his suffering. [4.6]
Thus, as he was traveling along the road with him,
a fiery chasm appeared before him;
having crossed over that blazing pit, [he proceeded].
He goes to the firm wooden fire of hell;
meanwhile, suddenly,
by the servants of Yama, who carry mallets, swords, and goads in their hands—
His entire body, beginning with the head, is crushed many times by mallets. [4.8]
False speech is blameworthy, its ripening is uneven and bitter;
it should be avoided by the wise as it produces terror in all people.
Speech should be spoken that is truthful and flows with the sweetness of honey.
The Victor’s tongue is indeed beneficial speech; it is always beneficial, worthy of being accepted, and divine.
(4.9) — Thus, in the *Daśākuśalakarmaphalaniścaya* (The Determination of the Results of the Ten Unwholesome Actions), composed in the Śikhariṇī meter.
The fourth chapter: An Exposition on the Results of False Speech. || o ||
Driven by the wind of his own committed karma, he wanders swiftly through the ten directions in hell.
Like a leaf stirred by the wind, Piśunaka follows him; alas, the servants of Death and the End follow after him as well. [5.1]
Then, having seized him and thrown him down, they slowly pulled away his girth-rope.
In that place, which extends for three hundred yojanas and is filled with hundreds of fruits accompanied by bulls, he quickly becomes deluded. [5.2]
Then, together with the henchmen of Yama who hold swords in their hands, he splits that [body] from one side all the way down to the hooves.
It is devoured by dogs,
jackals, and wolves, as well as by the flocks of ospreys, owls, and herons. [5.3]
Why do you not take a stand?
Your body consumed by the fire of calamity,
you weep with faltering words and lamentations.
What good have I not done while lamenting? Truly, being without refuge, whom shall I now approach for shelter? [5.4]
"Thinking, 'At that time, there will be nothing for him as a refuge to carry him across the great ocean of the sufferings of hell,' he himself, with a purified mind,"
A compassionate person ought to be so:

knowing that speech which causes division among others, which inflames the fire of anger, which is untrustworthy, unrighteous, and discordant, leads to the aforementioned results, one should not utter it.

Even for embodied beings who have become divided, that which binds them together most effectively and purposefully must be called "the virtuous"; those who possess such people shall be an indivisible community and worthy of honor. [5.6] (Śārdūlavikrīḍita)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the exposition on the fruits of malicious speech, within the Determination of the Fruits of the Ten Unwholesome Actions. ||o||
In hell, the servants of Yama torment one who utters words that pierce the vital organs of others.
Having struck him down with sharp blows,
his tongue is torn out by those razor-sharp weapons. [6.1] (Aupacchandasika meter)
Having shown it to him with its saliva of blood and entrails dripping out,
they said to him, "He has already eaten this.
Then he too, overcome by hunger—
How can he consume these things placed within his own mouth by them?
Furthermore, his very tender tongue, though repeatedly cut away, grows back again after a long time.
Thus, by the power of his own karma, he again undergoes intense suffering; his limbs are utterly exhausted by excruciating pain. [6.3]
The wretched one cries out and writhes intensely; even though he undergoes thousands of calamities in this way, the fire of his suffering does not go out. [6.4]
Then, as his pupils rolled, his eyes flowing with tears, and his vital breaths rising upward,
the messengers of Yama appeared before him, their purpose made clear.
They recite the verse of the virtuous simultaneously. [6.5] Verse:
Those sharp arrows of speech discharged by you from the bow of the tongue—
the harshness that was seen [in your past]— this is the fruit that has now arrived. [6.6]
Thus it is said.
Thus, abandoning harsh speech, the wise man, skilled in the welfare of others, should utter pleasant words;
for such a noble one becomes the sole kinsman of the world.
The son of the Sugata, speaking kindly with a clear mind—
this is from the *Puṣpitāgrā* in the *Daśākuśalakarmaphalaniścaya*.
The sixth chapter: The Exposition of the Fruit of Harsh Speech. || 0 ||
When the mouths of people are opened wide, many base individuals repeatedly throw into them great quantities of boiling copper.
For one who has gone to hell, that [flame] first burns the tongue,
then the throat, then the heart, and thereafter the entire intestine. [7.1] *nardataka/kokilaka*
Then that very [fire] burns the region of the colon; having instantly scorched the jaggery, it exits by that same path,
while the patient’s eye-sockets are rolling from the influence of the poison of distress.
That person also rolls about, wails, departs, and sinks down.
[7.2] These two auspicious verses concern one who flees without having severed [the bonds].
The messengers of Yama, who know the deeds performed in the past, recite:
"Indeed, many words of an incomparable nature were previously spoken by you; this is now that fruit of yours, brought forth loudly by him. [7.3]
Two *troṭaka* verses.
This fruit has come to you for that which was spoken by you— words that were disconnected, meaningless, incoherent, and unbound,
and which were never truthful, being constantly devoted only to the recitation of texts. [7.4]
That which is not [the tongue] is not seen by the wise as the tongue; it is merely a piece of flesh. [7.5]
Thus it is said.
A wise person, having directly understood that idle chatter is the cause of intense suffering,
should abandon it and speak words that exceedingly benefit sentient beings.
One who speaks of Brahman should be dear; by that, the world [is won].
[7.6] This is called *bhujaṅgaprayāta* in the *Daśākuśalakarmaphalaniścaya*.
The seventh chapter: An Exposition on Frivolous Speech. || 0 ||
The hell-being, dwelling in the houses and courtyards of others,
suffers manifold forms of misery regarding their wealth.
One perceives that which arises from one's own performed karma,
like a reflection appearing within the surface of a mirror.
[8.1] (Svāgatā)
Thus it occurs to him after he has closely examined it:
"May this entire collection of wealth be mine";
being overcome by craving, he is deluded.
He runs after much wealth;
therein, his mind permeated by greed, he perceives every object as a source of harm.
And one who wishes to enter the waters of the ocean of suffering would begin to seize wealth;
such is the case for that person of wicked mind, with [the wealth] in the palm of his hand.
A sharp sword has appeared;
others besides the denizens of hell follow it, their hands marked by arrows and filled with rage. [8.4]
Then, seeing them approaching, that evil one, with the fire of his blazing anger, slays them with his arrows.
They too, with their swords, [struck] him all at once.
Alas, they strike and devour his flesh;
even when his body is reduced to mere bones, at that time his longing for wealth does not subside.
In this way, many hundreds of years pass,
yet there is no refuge nor any pacification of his suffering.
Before such a person as this, the servants of Yama speak.
The verse, which contains words of true meaning and illuminates the fruits of those actions.
[8.7] Verse.
"Upon seeing the prosperity of others, the thought occurred to me: 'May it be mine! The fruit of that poison arising from covetousness has now arrived. [8.8]
Thus [it is said].
Those endowed with the intention of renouncing covetousness should give the best of their wealth to those who ask;
the Fully Awakened Ones, who have conquered all faults, are to be honored.
By that, those gods would be happy. [8.9]
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the exposition on the fruit of covetousness, in the *Daśākuśalakarmaphalaniścaya* (The Determination of the Fruits of the Ten Unwholesome Actions). || o ||
Afflicted by powerful enemies born of hell, produced by one's own evil deeds;
He departs together with that by which the tawny ones prevail;
by that, the hundred-eyed one possesses horses blazing with light. [9.1] (Pramitākṣarā meter)
For he is pierced by sharp arrows as he is pursued by enemies not far away;
his pair of feet is scorched by fires.
As he lies fallen upon the ground in agony,
his testicles are bitten by venomous snakes,
while his hips are devoured by *kaṭitaṭakaṅkiris*.
The belly was devoured by beasts of prey and lions, both those with manes and those without; the head was consumed by powerful and fierce dogs.
Thus, the intention to harm living beings was cast out by the noble ones.
A wise person seeking auspicious results should certainly not produce that [anger] even in a dream;
one who desires to perform favor for the world should give rise to it [only in the appropriate manner].
White as the great moon, the delighter of the mind,
he wandered through the sky, honored by the gods and the *apsarases*. [9.4]
Listening well to a song composed with graceful cadence,
he wanders about in a vehicle that rivals the palaces of the Lord of the Thirty-three Gods and is adorned with fine tinkling bells.
Having ascended a divine vehicle, radiant as the rays of the sun, [he departed]. [9.5]
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the exposition on the fruit of malice, within the Determination of the Fruits of the Ten Non-Virtuous Actions. || o ||
One who has gone to a state of misery wanders swiftly through misfortune; having died, the evil one roams like a *preta*.
Emaciated by hunger, with sunken eyes, his body is grey with dust stirred up by the force of the wind.

If one afflicted by thirst, with a parched palate, while pursuing water, should see a lake at a distance with blooming lotuses and rush toward it only to find it turbid with matted hair; therefore, having seen a river flowing with pure water and the force of rolling waves—
The one with the view of nihilism goes on, his body drenched by drops of sweat from his exertion, thirsting;
when he begins to drink, it turns out to be full of pus, consisting of the blood of worms—alas, everything would be in vain! Seeing this, he falls down, despairing, crying out. [10.2]
Seeing the celestial vault and the clouds, his body exhausted, he longs for them;
yet at that time, a shower of fierce rays, harsh bricks, and the like falls upon his limbs.
Rising again and again, he falls to the ground, helpless, his movements destroyed by terror.
Distressed by that affliction, he falters on the path upon seeing a similar person who had previously gone there;
slowly approaching the middle of the grove from afar to soothe his weariness, he sits down in tranquility, yet even there he is pierced by sharp leaves resembling swords and arrows.
Going along, desiring water that is not there, being bitten by brindled dogs,
he helplessly enters a high, blazing house of fire produced by his own karma;
therein, with a wretched mind, he is burned by intense, flaming masses of fire.
Emitting a terrible roar, with the flanks of his belly bursting open and his bones and flesh falling apart, he thus wanders for a thousand years through various kinds of sufferings;
therefore, the elders should awaken this entire world to the fact that it is indeed the inheritance of one's own karma. [10.5]
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the exposition on the fruit of wrong view, in the *Daśākuśalakarmaphalaniścaya*. || 0 ||
Each unwholesome act individually burns [the mind] and brings about suffering; how much more so when all of these are practiced together?
Therefore, the wise person should abandon all unwholesome deeds.
One who is happy might perform auspicious deeds, yet they would not be beneficial without [the Dharma].
[11.1] Mother, father, kinsmen, sons, wife, friends, clothing, food, drink, wealth, grain, houses, and land—
Beholding one's own body as flickering and unstable as a plantain leaf shaken by the wind, one should practice the fourfold dharma.
By means of dharma, the powerful king shines like the Lord of the Gods in heaven.
By means of dharma, the lord of kings is a universal monarch on earth;
by means of dharma, his feet are rubbed by the crest-jewels of excellent serpents.
Therefore, virtuous people should not deviate from dharma even for the sake of their own welfare. [11.3]
Likewise, from the noble Dharma, one attains the state of an Arhat;
also the sublime state of a Pratyekabuddha,
and even the unsurpassed, peaceful enlightenment here.
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be obtained through the Dharma. The Omniscient One has always taught that even great merit performed without faith does not bear fruit.
Therefore, one who recognizes virtue should generate supreme faith,
for faith is indeed the root in the accomplishment of Dharma,
as long as old age and disease do not arrive. [11.5]
As long as the power of the senses remains unimpaired,
and as long as life does not reach its exhaustion, so long, O noble ones, listen to the well-spoken words of the Jina. [11.6]

Extracted from the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna*, this has been written by me for the sake of my own mindfulness regarding the fruit arising from the ten unwholesome actions. Whatever pure merit has arisen from this—
By this [merit] of mine, which is as pure as the rays of the autumn moon and dispels the afflictions, may all beings become possessors of perfect awakening, virtuous lords of sages. [11.8]
May the clouds release water as they desire,
may the earth be endowed with abundant crops,
and may the king protect his subjects who bow before him.
"May I too truly attain supreme awakening.

[11.9] Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the general exposition of the fruits, concerning the fruit of abstaining from the seven [of the ten] unwholesome actions within the determination of the fruits of the ten unwholesome actions. || o ||
Thus ends this treatise entitled *The Fruits of the Ten Unwholesome Actions*. || 0 ||
This work is by the illustrious Divākarendra. Thus ends [the colophon].
This is the work of Divākara-candra.
It belongs to the glorious Mañjughoṣa, whose body possesses the splendor of ten million suns, who bears the crest-jewel of the True Dharma,
and whose radiance is tawny like the finest saffron paste.
May that sword always protect you— resplendent with a luster like the shimmering petals of a freshly blooming blue lotus, sharp, and possessing bristling scales of the color of molten gold.
[End of NAK manuscript] 117 verses.
